title: The Oil Was Never the Miracle
paragraphs:
The Oil Was Never the Miracle
The Forgotten Meaning of Anointing with Oil—and Why So Many Christians Have Missed What God Was Actually Doing
A small bottle of oil sat on the shelf.
For years it had remained untouched.
Not because it was unimportant.
But because somewhere along the way, many believers began focusing on the oil itself and forgot the One the oil was pointing to.

Today, anointing oil is often treated as a spiritual object, a sacred substance, almost as if power lives inside the bottle. Some carry it everywhere. Some place it around their homes. Some anoint doors, vehicles, wallets, businesses, and possessions.
Yet one of the most important questions remains:
What did God actually mean when He commanded anointing with oil?
Because if we misunderstand the symbol, we may completely miss the Savior behind it.
And perhaps that is exactly where many of us are today.
Holding the symbol.
Missing the Person.
The story of anointing begins long before church services, prayer meetings, or modern Christianity.
In the Hebrew Scriptures, the primary word translated "anoint" is מָשַׁח (māšaḥ), meaning "to smear," "to rub," or "to consecrate by applying oil."
From this word comes מָשִׁיחַ (Mashiach)—"Messiah"—meaning "The Anointed One."
That changes everything.
The moment Scripture speaks about anointing, it is already pointing forward to Jesus Christ.
Anointing was never ultimately about oil.
It was about Him.
Kings were anointed.
Priests were anointed.
Sometimes prophets were anointed.
Not because oil made them powerful.
But because God was publicly marking them as belonging to Him.
The oil represented divine appointment.
Divine ownership.
Divine purpose.
When the prophet Samuel poured oil over David's head, the miracle was not in the liquid running down his face.
The miracle was that God chose a forgotten shepherd nobody expected.
A scandal became a calling.
A shepherd became a king.
A nobody became part of God's redemption story.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Psalm 23 hints at this reality when David later writes:
The overflowing life was not produced by oil.
It flowed from God's presence.
This pattern continues throughout Scripture.
In Exodus, priests were anointed before serving God.
The oil symbolized consecration.
Being set apart.
Being holy.
Being devoted to God's purposes.
The Hebrew idea of holiness was never merely moral perfection.
It meant being separated unto God.
Belonging completely to Him.
Yet even these Old Testament ceremonies were shadows pointing forward to a greater reality.
Then Jesus arrives.
And suddenly everything comes into focus.
The New Testament Greek word often associated with anointing is χρίω (chriō), meaning "to anoint."
From this word comes Χριστός (Christos).
Christ.
The Anointed One.
The Greek title "Christ" and the Hebrew title "Messiah" mean the same thing.
Jesus is God's ultimate Anointed One.
Every drop of oil in the Old Testament was ultimately pointing toward Him.
Every king.
Every priest.
Every prophet.
Every ceremony.
Every sacrifice.
Every symbol.
Every shadow.
All of it leads to Jesus.
This is why Luke 4:18 records Jesus reading from Isaiah:
"The Spirit of the Lord is upon Me, because He has anointed Me..."
The Greek text says:
Πνεῦμα Κυρίου ἐπ’ ἐμέ, οὗ εἵνεκεν ἔχρισέν με
"The Spirit of the Lord is upon Me, because He has anointed Me."
Notice something remarkable.
The true anointing was not oil.
It was the Holy Spirit.
The physical oil had always been pointing toward the spiritual reality.
The symbol was never meant to replace the substance.
Many believers today desperately seek a fresh anointing while forgetting the One who pours it out.
We chase experiences.
Moments.
Feelings.
Manifestations.
But Scripture repeatedly redirects our eyes back to Christ Himself.
The deepest anointing is not found in possessing oil.
It is found in possessing Christ.
The Apostle John writes:
The Greek word used here is connected directly to Christ's own anointing.
Believers participate in what Jesus Himself possesses.
Not because we are powerful.
But because we belong to Him.
This understanding also explains James 5:14:
"Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord."
Notice carefully.
The healing is not attributed to the oil.
The emphasis remains on prayer.
Faith.
The Lord.
The oil functions as a visible expression of dependence upon God.
Just as baptism points beyond water.
Just as communion points beyond bread and wine.
The power belongs to God alone.
Not the element.
Not the ritual.
Not the object.
Only Him.
And perhaps this is where the message becomes painfully personal.
Because many of us have spent years searching for spiritual power while neglecting spiritual surrender.
We wanted God's hand.
But not necessarily God's heart.
We wanted breakthrough.
But not repentance.
We wanted blessing.
But not transformation.
The truth is that anointing has always been connected to surrender.
The oil marked those who belonged to God.
Not those who merely wanted benefits from God.
Maybe that's why this message feels uncomfortable.
Because it exposes something deeper than theology.
It exposes us.
The hidden pride.
The secret compromises.
The sins nobody sees.
The wounds nobody knows.
The fears we disguise with religious language.
And yet this is exactly where the Gospel shines brightest.
Jesus is not intimidated by your failures.
He is not shocked by your past.
He is not surprised by your struggles.
The cross already accounted for them.
The blood of Christ speaks a greater word than your shame.
The Anointed One came for the broken.
For the weary.
For the scandalized.
For the addicted.
For the self-righteous.
For the doubter.
For the prodigal.
For people like us.
The entire story of Scripture is not about people climbing their way toward God.
It is about God descending toward sinners through Jesus Christ.
That is the Gospel.
That is grace.
That is redemption.
That is why every bottle of oil ultimately points to a Savior whose mercy never runs dry.
Maybe you've been carrying guilt for years.
Maybe nobody knows the battle you're fighting.
Maybe you've become skilled at looking spiritually healthy while privately feeling exhausted.
Jesus sees it all.
And He still invites you closer.
Not because you are worthy.
But because He is.
Not because you are strong.
But because He is.
Not because your story is clean.
But because He specializes in rewriting stories.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs.
If you desire to glorify God through this ministry, your support truly makes a difference.
One day every symbol will fade, every ceremony will end, every earthly object will pass away—but Jesus Christ, the true Anointed One, remains forever.
And the hands that were pierced for your sins are still reaching for you today.
